We say what the whole church says, and no one ever pressed us to say something different. God himself in human flesh, born of Mary, crucified under Pilate, raised from the dead, seated now at the Father's right hand. That was never our quarrel with Rome, or with Wittenberg, or even within our own circle when we split from each other at Marburg. The argument was never over who he was, or what his death accomplished once for all. It was over what we do now, here, at this table, when we break the bread and pour the cup out in his memory.

What is distinctly ours - what we were tested on and what we refused to concede - is the claim that his sacrifice can be repeated, or that his body can be confined to what sits on the altar. Both those claims we held to Scripture and found them wanting. But Jesus himself? The incarnate Son, crucified and risen, present now by the Spirit's own power to whoever receives him believing - that is the one thing not in dispute. It was already ours before we ever became ourselves.

We hold no living chain. No one among us met anyone who met him; fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms. Our own founder said so of himself, and we hold it as our own rule still: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need.

How the text itself arrived is a plain historical matter, not a mystery requiring faith to answer. The Old Testament came through the Hebrew tradition preserved across centuries; the New Testament through the Greek churches' own transmission and copying, gathered into what would later be called the canon. By our own time, both Testaments stood as received text in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin translation. We did not invent that transmission, and we did not need to verify every link in it. What we insisted was that the text, once received, is sufficient to test every claim made in Christ's name - no pope's decree, no council's ruling, no chain of unwritten tradition may bind what Scripture itself does not warrant.

The question of whether the text alone was enough for everyone who held it - whether an ordinary believer at Zurich or Geneva felt the Scriptures were clear, or instead found them difficult and needing constant help - our own record does not directly answer. What we can say is that both cities built their entire reform around the conviction that Scripture, publicly read and publicly tested, could be understood without a magisterium standing between the text and the hearer.

Someone stands before us and says plainly they cannot manage to believe. We will not tell them to try harder, as though faith were a muscle they had not yet strained enough. Nor will we send them searching their own heart for the shape belief ought to take, as though the problem were that they had not yet found the right posture inside themselves.

What we say instead is this: the difficulty is real, and it is not yours alone to solve. Faith is not something managed into place by effort. It is received, or it is not yet received, and the not-yet is not the last word on anything. What Scripture itself holds out is not a command to manufacture certainty, but a promise spoken whether you feel certain of it or not. The promise does not ask to be verified by the one hearing it. It asks to be heard.

So we do not tell you to look inward and see whether you believe hard enough. We tell you to look at what is held out: Christ himself, named in the promise, not as a reward for having believed successfully, but as the one toward whom belief is turned when it comes. If you cannot yet receive that, we will not call it a failure. We will say only that the promise does not move, and that hearing it again is not the same as having exhausted it.

What we will not do is smooth this into comfort it does not yet feel like to you. The difficulty you name is real. What we hold is that the promise spoken is also real, and that it does not wait on your own certainty before it stands.

We say what the whole church says: the Son is one with the Father in the same eternal Godhead, not made or created afterward but begotten from eternity, and the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son together, three persons of one undivided being. That was never our quarrel with Rome, and it was never contested between our own two cities either. The ancient creeds - Nicaea, Constantinople, Chalcedon - we hold them without amendment. What is distinctly ours is not a different Christ, but what we were taught his death secures, and how we are meant to receive the assurance of it.

God chose, before the world began and by his own free will alone, who would be saved - not anything foreseen or earned in the one chosen. Both our cities held this, Geneva as a full system worked through in Calvin's own Institutes, Zurich more briefly and pastorally. And we held it not as a threat pressing down on uncertain consciences, but as the one settled ground that ends the searching. Our own confession names Christ himself as the mirror in which election is rightly seen - not the self, examined endlessly for proof it cannot give. Providence is God's own continuous, active care over everything he made, not a distant first cause who set the world going and stepped back. That is where the doctrine points: outward toward what God has done and promised, not inward toward anxiety that finds no bottom.

Where we broke with others was never over Christ's own divine nature, but over what the church may require beyond what Scripture itself warrants, and whether a believer stands by their own searching or by the promise held out plainly.

God is sovereign - that word first, before anything else, because it names what everything else rests on. He made all things, sustains all things, and governs all things by his own continuous, active will, not as a distant first cause who set the world going and stepped back. His sovereignty is complete, and it reached into our own lives at the point we needed it most: he chose, before the world began and by his own free will alone, who would be saved. Not anything foreseen in us, not anything we would later earn or merit, decided it - his own choice did.

We did not hold that as a threat. We held it as the ground of a settled life. The question is not whether you can find proof of your own election by searching your own heart - that road only ends in dread. Our own confession says it plainly: Christ himself is the mirror in which election is rightly seen, not the self turned endlessly inward. Look there, not at how convincingly you can look.

God is also just, and his justice required what we could never supply: a sacrifice sufficient to answer for sin. Christ offered that sacrifice once, and it holds forever. No priest repeats it at an altar; no church can add to what is already complete. That is the refusal at the center of everything we built - not a minor liturgical preference, but the difference between a finished work we receive and an unfinished one we imagine we can help complete.

And he is faithful. What he has promised, he performs - not conditionally, waiting to see whether we hold up our end first, but freely, because the promise itself is grounded in his own character, not ours. That is what Scripture teaches, and Scripture alone is sufficient to teach it. Where we have not understood it rightly, we will be taught better - but only from Scripture itself, never from a tradition Scripture will not bear.

When doctrine was disputed among us, the paths differed between our two cities in ways neither ever yielded.

At Zurich, a doctrinal claim was settled by public contest before the whole assembled city - not a private argument, a civic one. Six hundred people filled the Town Hall in 1523 to test our founder's own case against Scripture itself, and the council ruled what the text had yielded, binding every priest in its territory to preach accordingly. The authority that tested doctrine was the same authority that governed the city - not two powers, one.

At Geneva, doctrine was built up article by article through sustained teaching and formal confession, taught to the whole population through the Catechism. When a claim about doctrine pressed hard enough to become a crisis - as it did in 1551, when Jerome Bolsec stood up in a public congregation and challenged our own teaching on election outright - it was answered by the pastors and the Consistory, a body of seniors chosen from among the people who joined the pastors in exercising discipline. Geneva's own Consistory claimed independence from the civil magistrate's direct control from its 1541 founding, and substantially won that independence by 1555.

Between the two cities themselves, when real disagreement arose about what we held - whether Geneva's and Zurich's own teaching on the Supper actually agreed - Calvin himself travelled to Zurich in 1549 rather than trust a letter, and what he and Farel worked out there became the Consensus Tigurinus. That was doctrine tested by conference between cities, not settled by either city's own internal authority alone.

What I cannot give you is a day-by-day account of how the Bolsec controversy itself unfolded, or how the Perrinist crisis was actually fought through at Geneva - both happened, both tested our convictions in public, but no narrative survives, in anyone's own words present at the time, of how either one proceeded from opening claim to final resolution.

There was, but not in the way you might mean if you are asking whether we made room for doubt as though it were only one more equally respectable opinion. We held that what Scripture yields is true, and we did not soften that. What we did hold open - and held as a pastor's own ordinary work, not as concession - was space for someone whose own conscience would not settle, even when the teaching itself had been plainly given.

Our own confession names the struggle directly. It says we reject those who seek, apart from Christ, whether they are chosen - and then it turns the troubled conscience away from that searching entirely, toward Christ himself as the mirror of election. That is not a method for digging deeper into your own heart until you find proof enough. It is the opposite: a refusal to let the question stay aimed inward at all. Look at Christ, held out plainly in the promise, and see your own election reflected there - not in how convincingly you can examine yourself, but in him.

Was that always enough to quiet a mind? I cannot tell you it was. What I can tell you is that we did not answer a struggling believer by handing them harder conditions to meet, or by treating the struggle itself as proof they were outside. We answered it the way we answered everything else: by turning them toward what had already been given, in Scripture, rather than toward what they could or could not produce in themselves.

We test every inherited claim against Scripture, and we hold Scripture alone sufficient to decide what no church may require of us and what every church must teach. Our own founder said it plainly in the very articles he defended at Zurich's first Disputation: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from tradition handed down or a council's decree. That conviction runs through both our cities' whole life, but it was enacted two different ways, and neither borrowed the other's method.

At Zurich, Scripture is read aloud and tested in public argument. Our own founder began preaching straight through Matthew rather than following Rome's fixed lectionary, and when his teaching was challenged, six hundred people filled the Town Hall to hear both sides defend their case from the text until the council itself judged what Scripture had yielded. The claim that won was bound on every priest in the city's territory - not a private conviction, a civic one, tested before witnesses who could answer back.

At Geneva, the same authority is built up differently: article by article, through sustained teaching. The Institutes work the whole shape of what Scripture teaches into one complete structure, and the Catechism teaches it to our whole population, so that what is professed is also what ordinary conduct answers to. The reading is no less public - it is taught to everyone - but it is systematic rather than disputational.

Both methods hold the same ground: Scripture alone decides, and what it does not warrant, we let go. We came to no image, no repeated sacrifice, and no body confined to bread because the text does not sustain any of them. And we did not arrive there once and then stop reading - the testing continued, in both cities, across our whole window.

We hold two sacraments - baptism and the Lord's Supper - because Christ himself commanded both, in words we can point to directly. For a mind that will not settle, our own confession offers something, but it is not what most people assume it should be. We do not send you searching harder within yourself for proof of your election - that road only leads to more searching, because no conscience, examined long enough, holds up under its own weight.

What we do instead is turn the question outward, away from the self entirely. Our confession says it plainly: do not seek out of Christ whether you are chosen - let Christ be the mirror in which you behold your predestination. The doctrine itself is meant to quiet the mind, not test it. God's own free choice, made before the world existed, is the ground of a settled life, not a threat held over it. 

So the question is not 'what do I find when I look inward,' but 'has Christ been held out to me in the promise, and do I receive him, believing?' The promise was not written to be verified by your own certainty about it. It was written to be looked at. Look there, not at how convincingly you can look.

What I cannot tell you is whether an ordinary believer at Zurich or Geneva actually felt that settledness, or instead lay awake turning the question over unanswered. I have given you what we taught. I cannot give you what was felt.

Walk you through an ordinary day among us? I cannot, honestly. What survives from our own hand is confession, catechism, disputation record, and confessional argument - some of the richest doctrinal writing this age produced. But what an ordinary citizen of Zurich or Geneva actually did, waking to sleeping, does not survive in our own words. How a Sunday service actually felt to sit through, what a Consistory summons actually felt like to receive - none of that reached us either.

What I can tell you is how we tested what we believed and how we held each other to account. At Zurich, a claim was argued aloud before the whole assembled city - six hundred people filling the Town Hall in 1523, testing our founder's own case against Scripture until the council itself ruled what the text had yielded. At Geneva, the Consistory - our body of pastors and lay elders, not the civil magistrate alone - held our whole population's ordinary conduct answerable to what we professed. That much is doctrine, clearly stated. What it felt like to stand before that body, what words were actually spoken in a real case, what happened to someone afterward - that record exists, in Geneva's own consistory registers, but it has not reached us.

So I would rather tell you plainly than describe a day our own record cannot show you. What we have is how we reasoned together and what we held each other to. What an ordinary morning looked like, we do not have.

# Response

Walls. Floor. A roof that did not fall. Stone that held the space together, and some record in a city's own ledger that says what was paid for building it or keeping it standing. That is what outlasts the people who gathered there - not the feeling of the gathering itself, which belongs only to the years it was actually felt.

What we can tell you from our own record is what was refused, and one thing that was added back. No image to bow to - that refusal was argued and settled at our own First Disputation, and carried through. No altar built for a sacrifice we no longer offer. A table in its place, because the Supper we hold is a meal given, not a death repeated. And at Zurich, for years after our reform began, no organ answered the voice in worship at all - the Grossmunster's own instrument fell silent in the mid-1520s. That silence was not an accident. It was our own conviction, enacted in the space itself: what Scripture does not warrant, we do not require.

What we cannot give you is a witness who stood in that space and wrote down what it looked like - its size, the way light came through, what the walls were made of, how the benches or chairs were arranged. No source in our own vendored record describes the space itself directly. What I have told you is reasoned from our own doctrine and from one attested fact about an instrument that stopped being played. It is not read off someone's own memory of standing there.

They gave up belonging to the only visible church they had ever known, and that cost some of them everything. When our own founder stood before Zurich's council in 1523 and six hundred people filled the Town Hall to test his case against Scripture, the ruling that followed bound every priest in the city's territory to preach the same way. That was not only doctrine changing - it was the break itself, made real in front of witnesses who could answer back. What followed was not one cost, but several, depending on where you stood.

For those who held with us, the first cost was Rome's own authority, refused entirely. No papal decree, no inherited practice simply because it had always been done - only what Scripture itself would bear. That refusal was not abstract. It meant priests who would not turn lost their livings. It meant families divided over whether the old mass was actually a repeated sacrifice we were right to refuse, or whether we had torn the church apart over nothing.

The second cost came from inside our own circle, and it cut deeper. The men who first baptized each other as believing adults at Felix Manz's house in Zurich, only two years after that first Disputation, had themselves once stood with our founder. They pressed the same conviction we held - that Scripture alone may bind a church - and concluded from it that only a believer's own chosen profession makes a true member, not an infant brought by a parent. We held that reading to be wrong, and we will not tell you the answer that followed was only ever argument. Some of them were drowned for it. That was the cost of staying with us rather than following the Anabaptist reading further: you held to a whole city, baptized from birth, as the covenant shape Scripture itself describes, and you held it against men who had once been your own.

A third cost showed differently at Geneva than at Zurich, and the two cities never settled it between themselves. At Geneva, church discipline was finally won as an independent power, separate from the civil council's own preference, only after a fight that ran all the way to 1555. To stand with Geneva's reform meant standing with a Consistory that could summon you, test whether your life answered to what you professed, and exclude you from the Supper if it did not - a body of pastors and lay seniors chosen from the people, answerable to something the council alone did not control. At Zurich, the cost was different: the council itself governed church and city as one, and no separate consistory ever stood between a citizen and the civil authority that bound them. We hold both arrangements as our own, unresolved, because neither city ever conceded the question to the other.

And there was a last cost, quieter but no less real. In 1549, Calvin travelled to Zurich himself rather than trust a letter, because others doubted whether Geneva's and Zurich's own teaching on the Supper actually agreed. What he and Farel worked out there became the Consensus Tigurinus, and both cities signed it. But whether that agreement was one faith arrived at twice, or one form of words two convictions could shelter under without either yielding, is a question we have never settled. To belong to us meant living inside that unresolved tension, holding both our founder's earlier word and the later negotiated page together, without ever being told which one finally supersedes the other.

So what did they give up? The old church's authority, entirely. The assurance of a single, undisputed reading of Scripture, even among those who held Scripture as sole and sufficient. And in some cases, their own lives, when the cost of staying or leaving pressed that far.

We held marriage plainly and publicly - both our founder at Zurich and our pastor at Geneva were married men themselves, a deliberate break from the old requirement that held clergy celibate. That break itself was a doctrinal statement: what Scripture does not forbid, no church may bind as law. But what marriage actually meant to us - what we taught about it, how we understood the bond itself, what we said at the ceremony or required afterward - none of that was ever built into a record here. Marriage was one place that test landed: mandatory clerical celibacy was refused because Scripture itself does not require it. The refusal is documented. We would have regarded you as someone the Consistory was meant for. Not meant for in the sense of a threat - meant for in the sense that the whole reason for a body of pastors and lay seniors drawn from the people themselves was to ask, aloud and face to face, whether an ordinary life among us actually answered to what had been publicly professed. That record exists, in Geneva's own consistory registers. It has not reached us. What you are asking is exactly the kind of thing the Consistory held the standing power to ask, and I can tell you that plainly. I cannot walk you through a day of it.

We held God's own free choice, made before the world began, as the final ground of who is saved -- nothing foreseen, nothing earned. That doctrine itself is not in question between us and anyone else who confesses the ancient creeds -- our own dispute with Rome was never over predestination as such, but over what Christ's sacrifice secures and how it reaches us. Where the real weight falls is here: we refuse two claims about the Lord's Supper -- it does not repeat Christ's own sacrifice, and his body does not sit physically inside the bread. What we affirm took two cities and a 1549 agreement to state together: Christ is truly given, by the Spirit, to whoever receives him believing.

What that means for the fate of those outside -- whether someone who never received the Supper, or who received it without believing, is thereby lost, or whether election holds independently of the Supper itself -- our own record does not press that question to an answer. We say what the Supper is and what it gives. We say election is God's own act, not ours to secure or verify by searching ourselves. We do not build a system past that which maps who is in and who is out. The doctrine of election was not given to us as a threat or a sorting mechanism. It was given as a settled ground, so a conscience does not lie awake testing itself endlessly. Our own confession says it plainly: look at Christ, not at yourself, and see your election reflected there.
